query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a ceramic or other oxide-based coating to the surface of Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can improve its oxygen resistance without sacrificing its mechanical performance.
generation.intervention: Applying a ceramic or other oxide-based coating to the alloy surface
generation.conditions: High-temperature, oxidizing atmosphere, strain rate of 10−4–10−2 s−1
generation.mechanism: Prevention of oxygen penetration into the alloy
generation.predicted_outcome: 20-30% increase in room-temperature tensile ductility and 10-20% increase in yield strength at 1000 °C
generation.boundary: Temperature: 1000 °C, Atmosphere: Oxidizing, Exposure time: 100 hours, Mechanical-loading: Tensile testing
generation.uncertainty: The actual increase in ductility and yield strength may vary depending on the specific coating material and application method

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile testing of coated and uncoated HfNbTaTiZr samples at 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated sample shows less than 10% increase in tensile ductility and less than 5% increase in yield strength compared to the uncoated sample, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The NbTaHfTiZr HEA has received a lot of interests among all RHEAs, since it has a totally disordered BCC solid-solution structure with a melting point of about 1800 °C [,]. At normal temperature and cryogenic temperatures, the NbTaHfTiZr RHEA combines excellent strength and ductility []. The NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA based on this alloy not only maintains excellent room-temperature plasticity but also further improves its strength and has a good cold workability []. In order to explore the potential of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA for high-temperature applications, it is very necessary to study its mechanical properties at high temperatures. Here, we explore the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy from RT to 1227 K and analyze its microscopic deformation mechanism. At the same time, we construct the constitutive equation of this alloy through a stress–strain curve in a deformation temperature range of 873–1173 K and a 0.001–0.1 s−1 strain-rate range and quantify the relationship between the strength and temperature.

This indicates that the oxidative effect was not severe. Second, it may be due to a precipitation at high temperatures. The significant decrease in ductility at 1073 K is similar to that found in the TiZrHfNbTa alloy []. The precipitates from the grain boundary can damage the plasticity of the alloy. However, a previous analysis showed that the alloy had a single-phase BCC structure, and no precipitation was found by TEM. The possible reason is that the size of these precipitates was small, only a few nanometers in size, and it took a considerable time to find them in the field of view of TEM. This phenomenon will be the subject of another study. The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
